beats.say: In how many ways can 28 be written as a sum of two odd numbers?

board.text: 28 = odd number + odd number. How many ways?

beats.say: Notice what it wants. Not one sum, but a count: how many different pairs of odd numbers add up to 28.
The secret of counting is to go in order. Start with the smallest odd number, 1. 1 plus what makes 28? 27, and 27 is odd. That is our first pair.
Next odd number, 3. 3 plus 25. Then 5 plus 23. See the pattern? One side goes up by 2, and the other comes down by 2.
Keep going the same way. 7 plus 21. 9 plus 19. 11 plus 17. 13 plus 15.
The next one would be 15 plus 13. Should we count it?

choices: yes, it is a new pair
yes, and go on up to 27 + 1
ask.ifNot: 15 plus 13 uses the same two numbers as 13 plus 15, only swapped round. It is the same pair, so we stop here.

beats.say: So we stop, and count the lines on the board. 7 pairs, so 7 ways.
A quick check. Our first numbers were 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 and 13: every odd number below 14, which is half of 28. That is 7 numbers.
Careful: 14 is a tempting answer. But pairs like 2 plus 26 use even numbers, so they do not count.
So to count ways, list them in order, smallest first, and stop when the pairs begin to repeat. That gave us our 7.
Add the difference of 7369 and 2418 to their sum. Let's find the result.

board.text: Add the difference of 7369 and 2418 to their sum

beats.say: This sentence is a little tangled, so let's untangle it. It wants two things made first, a difference and a sum. Then those two are added together.
Start with the difference. Which operation finds a difference?

ask.ifNot: The difference is how far apart two numbers are. We find it by subtracting the smaller from the bigger.

beats.say: 7369 minus 2418. Work column by column from the ones, and regroup at the hundreds. We get 4951.
Now their sum. 7369 plus 2418. Remember to carry 1 from the ones column. That gives 9787.
Last step: add the difference to the sum. 4951 plus 9787 is 14738.
Now look closely at our lines. In one we took 2418 away, and in the other we added 2418. What do you think happens to the 2418 overall?
It cancels out! Taking 2418 away and adding it back leaves nothing. So all that remains is 7369, two times. And 2 times 7369 is 14738.
Isn't that neat? The difference of two numbers plus their sum is always twice the bigger number. It makes a fast check.
6 years hence, Sumit will be 17. Hence is an old word for from now. And we are asked how old he was 8 years ago.
Notice something. We are told about the future, and asked about the past. But nobody has told us his age today.
So what should we find first?

ask.ifNot: Both clues are counted from today: 6 years from now, and 8 years ago. So today's age is the bridge between them.

beats.say: Today's age, plus 6 more years, makes 17. So today he is 17 minus 6, which is 11.
Now go back 8 years. Which number do we take the 8 away from?

ask.ifNot: 8 years ago is counted from today, and today he is 11. So it is 11 minus 8.

beats.say: 11 minus 8 is 3.
So 8 years ago, Sumit was 3 years old.
Check by walking forward in time. He was 3. 8 years later he is 11, and that is today. 6 more years and he is 17. It all fits.
The trap was 17 minus 8, which jumps straight over today. In age questions, find the age now first, then move forward or back.
The ages of Disha and Nisha add up to 25 years today. What did their ages add up to 4 years ago?

board.text: Sum of their ages 4 years ago = ?

beats.say: Here is a puzzle. We don't know Disha's age, and we don't know Nisha's age. Only the total. Do you think it can still be done?
It can. We don't need each age, only how the total changes. Here is a bar for each girl, with the last 4 years marked off.

spec.note: Today the two bars add up to 25 years

beats.say: Going back 4 years, how much smaller is the sum of their ages?

ask.ifNot: Count the people. Disha was 4 years younger, and Nisha was 4 years younger too. That is 4 and 4, 8 years in all.

beats.say: Two girls, each 4 years younger. 2 times 4 is 8.
So take 8 away from the total. 25 minus 8 is 17.
Four years ago, their ages added up to 17 years.
Let's try it with real ages. Say Disha is 12 and Nisha is 13, which makes 25. Four years ago they were 8 and 9, and 8 plus 9 is 17.
The trap is taking the 4 away only once. When time moves, it moves for everyone, so multiply the years by the number of people.
In 2020, the ages of Mr Joshi, his wife and his son added up to 100 years. What will they add up to in 2028?
First, how much time goes by? From 2020 to 2028 is 8 years.
Here is the family as three bars. In those 8 years, every one of them has 8 more birthdays.

spec.note: In 2020 the three ages add up to 100

beats.say: So by how much does the sum of their ages grow?

ask.ifNot: Count the people: Mr Joshi, his wife and his son. All 3 of them get 8 years older, and 3 times 8 is 24.

beats.say: 3 people, 8 years each. 3 times 8 is 24.
Add that to the old total. 100 plus 24 is 124.
In 2028, their ages will add up to 124 years.
Look at the bars to check. Three extra pieces of 8: 8 plus 8 plus 8 is 24. And 100 plus 24 is 124.
The trap is adding the 8 only once. Every person gets older, so multiply the years by the number of people.
4 years from now, the ages of Vijay and Vinay will add up to 67 years. What did their ages add up to 5 years ago?

board.text: 5 years ago: sum of their ages = ?

beats.say: We have to travel in time twice. First from the future back to today. Then from today back into the past. Here is our time line.
First jump: from 4 years ahead, back to today. By how much does the sum of their ages drop?

ask.ifNot: There are two people, and each of them is 4 years younger today than in 4 years' time. 2 times 4 is 8.

beats.say: 2 times 4 is 8. So today their ages add up to 67 minus 8, which is 59.
Second jump: from today, back 5 years. How much does the sum drop this time?

ask.ifNot: Again there are two people. Each was 5 years younger, and 2 times 5 is 10.

beats.say: 2 times 5 is 10. And 59 minus 10 is 49.
So 5 years ago, their ages added up to 49 years.
Check with one big jump. From 4 years ahead to 5 years ago is 9 years. Two people, so the sum drops by 18. And 67 minus 18 is 49.
So in age questions, come back to today first. And remember that every year counts once for each person.
In 2015, the ages of Aman and Suman added up to 87 years. Aman celebrated his 37th birthday in 2005. In which year was Suman born?

board.text: Aman turned 37 in 2005. Suman born in ?

beats.say: That is a lot of years flying about! So let's make a plan. Aman's age in 2015, then Suman's age in 2015, then Suman's year of birth.

board.text: Plan: Aman in 2015, Suman in 2015, birth year

beats.say: Aman was 37 in 2005. So how old was he in 2015?

ask.ifNot: From 2005 to 2015 is 10 years. So Aman was 10 years older than 37, which is 47.

beats.say: 2015 minus 2005 is 10 years. And 37 plus 10 is 47. So Aman was 47 in 2015.
Now both facts are about 2015. Together they were 87, and Aman was 47. So Suman was 87 minus 47, which is 40.
Suman was 40 years old in 2015. So how do we find the year Suman was born?

ask.ifNot: Suman's age of 40 belongs to the year 2015. So we count 40 years back from 2015.

beats.say: Suman was born in 1975.
Check. Someone born in 1975 is 40 in 2015. And 40 plus 47 is 87. It fits.
The trap was mixing years: Aman's 37 belongs to 2005, but the 87 belongs to 2015. Bring every fact to the same year before you combine them.
A school starts the year with 1005 students. During the year 13 leave and 42 join. At the end, 1000 pass the final exam. How many did not pass?

board.text: 1000 passed. How many did not pass?

beats.say: The exam comes at the end of the year. So what must we know before we can answer?

choices: the number of students at the end
ask.ifNot: Only students who are in the school at the end can sit the exam. So first we need the number of students at the end of the year.

beats.say: Follow the story in order. 13 students left, so the number goes down. 1005 minus 13 is 992.
Then 42 joined, so the number goes up. 992 plus 42 is 1034. That is the school at the end of the year.
Now split those 1034 students into two groups: the ones who passed, and the ones who did not.
How do we find the missing piece of the bar?

ask.ifNot: The whole bar is 1034 and one piece of it is 1000. Take the piece we know away from the whole.

beats.say: So 34 students did not pass.
Check. 1000 who passed and 34 who did not make 1034, the school at the end of the year.
The trap was 1005 minus 1000, which forgets the children who left and joined. In a story sum, follow the story in order.
In a class there are 11 fewer boys than girls. There are 42 girls. What is the strength of the whole class?

board.text: Boys are 11 fewer than girls. Girls = 42.

beats.say: Strength just means how many students there are altogether, boys and girls. We know the girls. We don't yet know the boys.
Look at the bars. There are 11 fewer boys than girls. So how many boys are there?

spec.note: The boys' bar is shorter by 11

ask.ifNot: Fewer means a smaller number. The boys' bar is shorter than the girls' bar by 11, so we subtract.

beats.say: 42 minus 11 is 31. There are 31 boys.
Are we finished? Not yet! 31 is only the boys, and the question asks for the whole class. This is where many children stop too soon.
Girls and boys together: 42 plus 31 is 73.
The class has 73 students.
Check. 73 students, take away the 42 girls, leaves 31 boys. And 31 is 11 fewer than 42. Good.
So first find the group you don't know, then answer what was really asked. And remember, fewer means subtract.
A and B stood in an election. A received 275 votes, and B won by a majority of 35 votes. How many votes were cast altogether?

board.text: A got 275 votes. B won by 35 votes.

beats.say: Won by a majority of 35 means B got 35 more votes than A. Here it is as two bars.

spec.note: B has 35 more votes than A

beats.say: So how many votes did B get?

ask.ifNot: B is the winner, so B has more votes than A. 35 more than 275 means we add.

beats.say: 275 plus 35 is 310. B got 310 votes.
Careful now. 310 is only B's votes. The question asks for all the votes cast, A's and B's together.
So 585 votes were cast in the election.
Check with the bars. Two pieces of 275 make 550. Add the extra 35, and we get 585.
So always read what the question wants at the end. Here it was the total, so we needed both bars.
In a class of 40, 18 students have been to Delhi and 15 have been to Kashmir. 6 have been to both. How many have been to neither place?
Two overlapping groups, so let's draw two overlapping circles. The 6 children who have been to both places sit in the middle.
If we simply add the 18 and the 15, what happens to those 6 children in the middle?

ask.ifNot: The 6 are inside the Delhi 18, and inside the Kashmir 15 as well. So adding the two counts them two times.

beats.say: Let's add anyway, and then put it right. 18 plus 15 is 33, with the middle 6 counted twice.
Take the 6 away once, so every child is counted just one time. 33 minus 6 is 27. So 27 children have been to at least one place.
27 children are somewhere inside the circles, and the class has 40. How do we find the ones outside?

ask.ifNot: The children outside the circles are the rest of the class. So take the 27 inside away from all 40.

beats.say: 40 minus 27 is 13.
So 13 students have been to neither Delhi nor Kashmir.
Check by filling in the circles. Delhi only is 18 minus 6, which is 12. Kashmir only is 15 minus 6, which is 9. And 12, 6, 9 and 13 add up to 40.

spec.note: 13 students are outside both circles

beats.say: So with two overlapping groups: add them, take the overlap away once, then subtract from the whole class.
A class has 30 students, and every one speaks Hindi or Marathi, or both. 21 speak Hindi, and 5 speak both. How many speak only Marathi?

board.text: 30 students. Each speaks Hindi, Marathi or both.

beats.say: Two circles again. And notice: every student speaks at least one language, so nobody stands outside the circles.

spec.note: All 30 students are inside the circles

beats.say: The whole Hindi circle holds 21 students. Careful: that 21 already includes the 5 in the middle who speak both.
So which students are left outside the Hindi circle?

choices: the ones who speak only Marathi
ask.ifNot: Everyone speaks Hindi or Marathi. A student who is not in the Hindi circle must be in the part for Marathi only.

beats.say: So take the Hindi circle away from the whole class. 30 minus 21 is 9.
And we do not subtract the 5 again. They were already inside the 21. Taking them away twice is the trap in this question.
So 9 students speak only Marathi.
Check by filling in the circles. Hindi only is 21 minus 5, which is 16. Then 16, 5 and 9 add up to 30, the whole class.
So draw the circles, and ask what each number really covers. The 21 covered the whole Hindi circle, middle and all. That is how we reached 9.
Four players join a chess tournament. Each player plays one game against every other player. How many games are played in all?

board.text: 4 players. Each pair plays one game. Games = ?

beats.say: Let's give the players names: A, B, C and D. A game needs two players, so we are really counting pairs.
Start with A. A plays B, A plays C, A plays D. That is 3 games.

board.text: A plays B, C, D: 3 games

beats.say: Now B. Careful: B against A is already on our list. So how many new games does B have?

ask.ifNot: B's game against A is already counted. B's new games are against C and against D, which makes 2.

beats.say: B has 2 new games, against C and D. C has only 1 new game, against D. And D? Every one of D's games is already listed.

board.text: B plays C, D: 2 new games

beats.say: Add them up. 3 plus 2 plus 1 is 6. So 6 games are played in all.
Check another way. Each of the 4 players plays 3 games, and 4 times 3 is 12. But that counts every game twice, once for each player in it. Half of 12 is 6.
The trap is that 12. A against B and B against A are the same game. So list the pairs in order, and never count one twice.
At a meeting, 13 people all shake hands with each other. How many handshakes happen in all?

board.text: 13 people. Everyone shakes hands with everyone.

beats.say: 13 is a lot of people, so let's try a tiny meeting first, with 3 people: A, B and C. The handshakes are A with B, A with C, and B with C. That makes 3.

board.text: 3 people: AB, AC, BC make 3 handshakes

beats.say: Here is a quicker way to count the same thing. Each of the 3 people shakes 2 hands, and 3 times 2 is 6. But 6 is double the real 3, because each handshake got counted by both people in it.
Back to our 13 people. How many hands does each person shake?

ask.ifNot: Nobody shakes their own hand! So each person shakes hands with the 12 other people.

beats.say: 13 people, 12 handshakes each. 13 times 12 is 156.
Is 156 the number of handshakes?

choices: no, each one was counted twice
ask.ifNot: When A shakes hands with B, we counted it once for A and once again for B. One handshake, counted two times.

beats.say: So we halve it. 156 divided by 2 is 78.
There were 78 handshakes.
We can check by counting new handshakes person by person. The first person shakes 12 hands, the next has 11 new ones, then 10, and so on down to 1. Added up, that is 78 as well.
So for handshakes, or games between pairs: multiply each person by the others, then halve, because every pair was counted twice.
A factory makes 1720 boxes every day. What is its total production in the month of July?

board.text: 1720 boxes every day. Total in July = ?

beats.say: One number seems to be missing. To find the total for July, what else do we need to know?

ask.ifNot: July is one of the long months, with 31 days. On your knuckles, July lands on a knuckle, and knuckle months have 31.

beats.say: So the factory makes 1720 boxes, 31 times over. That is 1720 times 31. A big sum, so let's break the 31 into 30 and 1.
First the 30 days. 1720 times 3 is 5160. Put a zero on the end for times 30, and we have 51600.
Now the 1 extra day: 1720 more boxes. This is the day children forget!
Add the two parts. 51600 plus 1720 is 53320.
So in July the factory makes 53320 boxes.
Check. Take one day's boxes off our answer: 53320 minus 1720 is 51600, exactly the 30 days we began with.
The trap is to use 30 days and stop at 51600. So know your months, and split a hard multiplication into easy pieces.
12.5 kilograms of sweets are shared equally among 25 students. 17 of them are girls and the rest are boys. How much does each boy get?

board.text: 12.5 kg of sweets shared equally by 25 students
17 girls, the rest boys. Each boy gets = ?

beats.say: Read one word again: equally. So does a boy get more than a girl, less, or the same?

ask.ifNot: Equally means every student gets the same amount, whether a boy or a girl.

beats.say: So each boy gets the same as any other student. That means the 17 girls is extra information. We don't need it at all.
Now the sharing. 12.5 kilograms among 25 is awkward, so let's change to grams. 1 kilogram is 1000 grams, so 12.5 kilograms is 12500 grams.
Among how many students do we share the 12500 grams?

ask.ifNot: The sweets went to all 25 students, not only to the boys. So we share among 25.

beats.say: 125 divided by 25 is 5. So 12500 divided by 25 is 500.
Each boy gets 500 grams of sweets.
Check. 25 students with 500 grams each: 25 times 500 is 12500 grams, which is our 12.5 kilograms.
Two things to keep. Watch for the word equally. And don't be afraid to leave a number unused when the question does not need it.
A student was meant to multiply a number by 13. By mistake he divided it by 13, and got a quotient of 11 with remainder 4. What should the answer have been?
It is a little detective story, in two steps. First find the secret number he started with. Then do what he was supposed to do with it.

board.text: Step 1: find the number. Step 2: multiply by 13.

beats.say: We know the divisor, 13, the quotient, 11, and the remainder, 4. How do we rebuild the number?

ask.ifNot: The number is made of 13 groups of 11, and then the 4 that were left over. Left over means we add them back on.

beats.say: 13 times 11 is 143. Add the remainder: 143 plus 4 is 147. The secret number is 147.
We have the number, 147. Are we finished?

ask.ifNot: 147 is only the number he started with. The question asks what he should have got, by multiplying it by 13.

beats.say: So, 147 times 13. Split the 13 into 10 and 3. 147 times 10 is 1470. 147 times 3 is 441. And 1470 plus 441 is 1911.
So the correct answer to his problem was 1911.
Check our secret number. 147 divided by 13: 13 times 11 is 143, with 4 left over. Quotient 11, remainder 4, just as the question said.
So to undo a division: divisor times quotient, plus remainder. Then do what the question really wanted.
A basket has 56 apples. Amey takes out 4 apples at a time and puts 3 oranges in their place, until no apples are left. How many oranges are there at the end?

board.text: 56 apples. Each turn: 4 apples out, 3 oranges in.

beats.say: Each turn is a swap: 4 apples out, 3 oranges in. Watch the first few turns in this table.
The oranges go up by 3 on every turn. So if we know the number of turns, we know the oranges. The turns are the key.
How many turns does it take to remove all 56 apples?

ask.ifNot: Apples leave 4 at a time. So the number of turns is how many times 4 goes into 56.

beats.say: 56 divided by 4 is 14. So Amey makes 14 swaps.
Each of the 14 turns puts in 3 oranges. So how do we find the oranges?

ask.ifNot: 3 oranges go in on every turn, and there are 14 turns. 14 lots of 3 means multiply.

beats.say: 14 times 3 is 42.
So there are 42 oranges in the basket at the end.
Does that make sense? Each swap puts in one fruit fewer than it takes out. 14 swaps, so 14 fewer fruits, and 56 minus 14 is 42. Yes.
So when something happens again and again, first count how many times it happens. Then multiply.
Four years from now, Siya will be 3 years older than Diya. Today their ages add up to 35. How old is Siya now?

board.text: In 4 years Siya will be 3 years older than Diya
Now: Siya + Diya = 35 years. Siya now = ?

beats.say: In four years, Siya will be 3 years older than Diya. So how much older is she today?

ask.ifNot: Both girls grow older together, one year every year. So the gap between them never changes. It is 3 years today as well.

beats.say: Say it with me: the gap between two ages never changes. So Siya is 3 years older today too, and the four years was only there to distract us.
Now draw it. Diya's bar, and Siya's bar, which is the same length plus an extra 3. Together they make 35.

spec.note: Together the bars make 35 years

beats.say: Snip off Siya's extra 3, and what is left is two equal bars. 35 minus 3 is 32.
Those 32 years are two equal bars, and each one is Diya's age. How do we find Diya's age?

ask.ifNot: Two equal bars make 32, so one bar is half of 32.

beats.say: 32 divided by 2 is 16. Diya is 16. But careful, the question asks for Siya!
Siya is 3 years older than Diya. 16 plus 3 is 19.
So Siya is 19 years old now.
Check both clues. 19 plus 16 is 35, the sum. And 19 minus 16 is 3, the gap. Both work.
So when you know a sum and a gap: take the gap off, halve what is left, and add the gap back for the older one.
At a sports meet there were 14 events, with a gold, a silver and a bronze medal in each. The boys won 6 fewer medals than the girls. How many did the boys win?

board.text: 14 events. Gold, silver, bronze in each event.
Boys won 6 fewer medals than girls. Boys = ?

beats.say: The total number of medals is hiding in the first sentence. How do we find it?

ask.ifNot: Gold, silver and bronze: that is 3 medals in every event. 14 events with 3 medals each means 14 times 3.

beats.say: 3 medals in each of 14 events. 14 times 3 is 42 medals in all.
Now share the 42 between the boys and the girls. The girls' bar is the boys' bar plus an extra 6.

spec.note: Together the bars make 42 medals

beats.say: Snip off the girls' extra 6, and two equal bars are left. 42 minus 6 is 36.
36 is two equal bars, and each one is the boys' share. So how many did the boys win?

ask.ifNot: Two equal bars make 36, so one bar is half of 36. Halving the 42 would not work, because the two shares in 42 are not equal.

beats.say: 36 divided by 2 is 18.
The boys won 18 medals.
Check. The girls won 18 plus 6, which is 24. And 18 plus 24 is 42, all the medals.
So for a total and a difference: take the difference off first, then halve the rest to get the smaller share.
Jiya has the same number of 5 rupee, 10 rupee and 20 rupee notes. Altogether she has 910 rupees. How many notes of each kind does she have?

board.text: ₹910 in all. Notes of each kind = ?

beats.say: The key words are equal numbers. That means we can bundle the notes into sets, each set holding one 5, one 10 and one 20.
How much is one set worth?

ask.ifNot: Add the three notes in a set: 5 plus 10 plus 20. That makes 35 rupees.

beats.say: 5 plus 10 plus 20 is 35. Every set is worth 35 rupees.
Now, how many sets of 35 rupees make 910 rupees?

ask.ifNot: We are counting how many times 35 fits into 910. Dividing by 3 would treat all three notes as if they were worth the same.

beats.say: 35 times 20 is 700. That leaves 210, and 35 times 6 is 210. So 20 and 6 together: 26 sets.
Each set has one note of each kind. So 26 sets means 26 notes of each kind.
Check with the money. 26 fives are 130. 26 tens are 260. 26 twenties are 520. And 130 plus 260 plus 520 is 910.
So when there are equal numbers of different things, make one set, find its value, and count the sets.
Minal bought the same number of 5 paise, 20 paise and 25 paise stamps. She paid 9 rupees in all. How many stamps did she buy altogether?

board.text: Equal numbers of 5 p, 20 p and 25 p stamps

beats.say: The stamps are priced in paise, but she paid in rupees. So first, how many paise is 9 rupees?

ask.ifNot: 1 rupee is 100 paise. So 9 rupees is 9 times 100, which is 900 paise.

beats.say: 9 times 100 is 900. She paid 900 paise.
Equal numbers of each stamp, so bundle them into sets of three: one of each kind. One set costs 5 plus 20 plus 25, which is 50 paise.
How many sets of 50 paise can 900 paise buy? 900 divided by 50 is 18 sets.
So is 18 our answer?

ask.ifNot: The question asks for the total number of stamps. Each set holds 3 stamps, so we need 18 lots of 3.

beats.say: 18 sets, with 3 stamps in each. 18 times 3 is 54.
Minal bought 54 stamps.
Check with the money. 18 stamps at 5 paise is 90. 18 at 20 paise is 360. 18 at 25 paise is 450. And 90 plus 360 plus 450 is 900 paise.
So make the units match, build one set, and count the sets. Then read the question once more to see exactly what it asks for.
If six people eat 1 kilogram of rice in a day, how much rice will 24 people eat in a week?

board.text: 6 people eat 1 kg of rice in a day
24 people in a week eat ? kg

beats.say: Before any sum, spot what is different between the two lines. More people, and more days. Two changes, so we take them one at a time.
Start with the people, and keep it to one day. Picture the 24 people sitting in groups of six, each group around its own 1 kilogram of rice.

spec.note: Each group of 6 eats 1 kg in a day

beats.say: How many groups of six can 24 people make?

ask.ifNot: Ask how many times 6 goes into 24. 6 times 4 is 24, so there are 4 groups.

beats.say: 24 divided by 6 is 4. That is 4 groups with 1 kilogram each, so 24 people eat 4 kilograms in a day.
Now the days. Careful: a week is 7 days, not 5. People eat rice at the weekend too!
4 kilograms a day, for 7 days. What do we do?

ask.ifNot: The same 4 kilograms is eaten on each of the 7 days. 7 lots of 4 means multiply.

beats.say: 4 times 7 is 28. So 24 people eat 28 kilograms of rice in a week.
Check by doing the days first. Six people eat 7 kilograms in a week. 24 people is 4 times as many, and 7 times 4 is 28.
Two changes, two steps. Sort out the people, then the days, and never mix them up.
In a school there are 4 girls for every 7 boys, and one teacher for every 55 students. There are 455 boys. How many teachers are there?
This is a chain. Teachers depend on all the students, and for all the students we need the girls. So the plan is: girls, then students, then teachers.

board.text: Plan: girls, then all students, then teachers

beats.say: 4 girls for every 7 boys is the ratio 4 is to 7. As bars: the girls are 4 pieces, the boys are 7 pieces, and the boys' whole bar is 455.

spec.note: Every piece is the same size

beats.say: How do we find what one piece is worth?

ask.ifNot: The 455 are boys only, and the boys' bar has 7 pieces. So one piece is 455 divided by 7.

beats.say: 455 divided by 7 is 65. Notice we did not divide by 11, because 455 is not the whole school, only the boys.
The girls have 4 pieces. 4 times 65 is 260 girls.
Now all the students. 455 boys plus 260 girls is 715.
There is one teacher for every 55 students. How do we find the number of teachers?

ask.ifNot: Teachers are counted against all the students, girls and boys. So we count how many times 55 goes into 715.

beats.say: 55 times 10 is 550. That leaves 165, which is 55 times 3. So 715 divided by 55 is 13.
The school has 13 teachers.
Check the students another way. 4 pieces and 7 pieces make 11 pieces, and 11 times 65 is 715. It matches.
A long question is just short steps in a chain. Find one piece, build the total, then count the groups of 55 to reach our 13.
Diya is sharing out 39 toffees in the ratio 1 is to 2. Our job is to find the larger group.

board.text: 39 toffees in the ratio 1 : 2. Larger group = ?

beats.say: Let's read it like detectives. There is 39 to share. The ratio is 1 is to 2. And the question only wants the larger group.
A ratio of 1 is to 2 means this. One side gets 1 equal part, and the other gets 2 parts of the very same size. Here they are as two bars.

spec.note: Every piece is the same size

beats.say: Count the pieces in both bars. How many equal parts are there altogether?

ask.ifNot: Count every piece, in both bars. 1 and 2 together make 3 parts.

beats.say: Count the pieces in both bars. How many equal parts are there altogether?

ask.ifNot: Count every piece, in both bars. 1 and 4 together make 5 parts.

beats.say: 1 plus 4 is 5. So the whole 75 is cut into 5 equal parts.
Careful with this next step, it is the one that trips people up. What is one part worth?

ask.ifNot: The 75 fills all 5 parts, not just the 4 parts of one bar. So we divide 75 by 5.

beats.say: 75 divided by 5 is 15. Now we can write 15 on every piece of both bars.

spec.note: Each piece is worth 15

beats.say: The larger group has 4 of these parts. 4 times 15 is 60.
So the larger group has 60 stickers. There it is!
Let's check. The smaller group is just 1 part, which is 15. And 15 plus 60 is 75, the number we started with.
So, to share in a ratio: count the parts, find what one part is worth, then take as many parts as you need.
The ages of Kavya and Karan are in the ratio 4 is to 7. Karan is 56 years old, and we want Kavya's age.
Look at the order carefully. Kavya is named first, so Kavya goes with the 4. Karan is second, and goes with the 7.
As bars: Kavya's age is 4 equal parts, and Karan's is 7 parts of the same size. We know Karan's whole bar is 56 years.

spec.note: Every piece is the same size

beats.say: So how do we find what one part is worth?

ask.ifNot: The 56 years belong to Karan alone, and Karan's bar has 7 parts. So we divide 56 by 7.

beats.say: 56 divided by 7 is 8, so each part is 8 years. Notice we did not add 4 and 7 this time, because 56 is not the total of both ages.

spec.note: Each piece is 8 years

beats.say: Kavya has 4 of these parts. 4 times 8 is 32.
So Kavya is 32 years old.
Check. Take 32 is to 56, and divide both by 8. We get 4 is to 7, the ratio in the question.
Here is the plan to keep. Find one part from the age you know, then take as many parts as the other person has.
Diya is 39 years old and Nikhil is 20. We want the sum of their ages after 10 years.

board.text: Diya is 39, Nikhil is 20. Sum after 10 years = ?

beats.say: Read the last part again: after 10 years. So we don't add the ages they have today. We add the ages they will have then.
Here is a bar for each of them. In 10 years, each bar grows by a piece of 10.

spec.note: Both bars grow by the same piece

beats.say: Who gets older in those 10 years?

ask.ifNot: Time passes for everybody. Diya gets 10 years older, and so does Nikhil.

beats.say: Diya will be 39 plus 10, which is 49. Nikhil will be 20 plus 10, which is 30.
Now add the two new ages. 49 plus 30 is 79.
So after 10 years, their ages add up to 79.
Here is a quick check. Today they add up to 59. Two people each gain 10 years, so the sum gains 20. And 59 plus 20 is 79.
The slip to avoid is adding the 10 only once. Two people means the years are added two times.
Arjun is 47 years old and Riya is 42. The question asks for the difference in their ages 7 years ago.

board.text: Arjun is 47, Riya is 42. Difference 7 years ago = ?

beats.say: Difference means the gap between the two ages: how much older one of them is than the other.
Think about this before any sum. 7 years ago, was the gap between them bigger, smaller, or the same as today?

ask.ifNot: Both of them were 7 years younger then. They step back together, so the gap between them does not move.

beats.say: Here is a fact worth keeping: the gap between two ages never changes. Every year, both people get exactly one year older.

spec.note: The extra piece is the gap between them

beats.say: So we only need the gap today. Arjun's bar is Riya's bar plus an extra piece. 47 minus 42 is 5.
Don't just take my word for it. Go back 7 years: Arjun was 47 minus 7, that is 40. Riya was 42 minus 7, that is 35.
And 40 minus 35 is 5. The very same gap!
So 7 years ago, the difference in their ages was 5 years.
The 7 years was only there to tempt us into extra sums. For a difference in ages, past or future, just subtract the ages you are given.
A worker earns 3 rupees an hour for his first 40 hours. After that comes overtime, which pays twice as much. In all he was paid 168 rupees.

board.text: ₹3 an hour for the first 40 hours
Overtime pays twice as much. Total pay ₹168

beats.say: What are we hunting for? The number of overtime hours. So picture his pay as one bar with two pieces: regular pay and overtime pay.
Which of the two pieces can we work out straight away?

ask.ifNot: We know everything about the regular time: 40 hours, at 3 rupees an hour. So we start there.

beats.say: 40 hours at 3 rupees an hour. 40 times 3 is 120, so 120 rupees is his regular pay.
The rest of the 168 rupees must be overtime pay. 168 minus 120 is 48.
Now, how much does one hour of overtime pay? Remember, it is twice the regular 3 rupees.

ask.ifNot: Twice means 2 times. 2 times 3 rupees is 6 rupees for each overtime hour.

beats.say: 2 times 3 is 6. Careful here: the trap is to divide the 48 rupees by the regular 3. Overtime hours earn 6 rupees each.
So how many times does 6 go into 48? 48 divided by 6 is 8.
He worked 8 hours of overtime.
Check it. 8 hours at 6 rupees is 48. Add the regular 120, and we get 168, exactly what he was paid.
So when pay comes in two parts, work out the part you know, take it away, and then deal with what is left.
40 grams of talc powder costs 12 rupees. We want the cost of 70 grams of the same powder.
Same powder, so every gram costs the same. But 70 grams is not double 40 grams, or any neat number of times 40. So there is no quick jump.
So what is the smart thing to find first?

ask.ifNot: When the numbers don't fit neatly, find the cost of 1 first. From 1, we can reach any number.

beats.say: One gram costs 12 rupees shared over 40 grams. Careful: that is 12 divided by 40, not 40 divided by 12. We are sharing rupees among grams.
12 divided by 40 is 0.30. So 1 gram costs 0.30 rupees, which is 30 paise.
We have one. Now, how do we get to 70 grams?

ask.ifNot: Each gram costs 0.30 rupees, and there are 70 of them. 70 lots of the same amount means multiply.

beats.say: 70 times 0.30 is 21. Think of it as 7 times 3.
So 70 grams costs 21 rupees.
Check another way. 10 grams cost 10 times 0.30, which is 3 rupees. 70 grams is 7 lots of 10 grams, and 7 times 3 is 21. Same answer.
That is the unitary method: find one, then find many.
12 buckets can hold 108 litres of water. How many buckets do we need to store 162 litres?
What do we want? A number of buckets, not litres. And every bucket is the same size, so let's line up what we know.
What should we find first?

ask.ifNot: Find one first. Once we know what 1 bucket holds, any number of litres is easy.

beats.say: 108 litres shared equally among 12 buckets. 108 divided by 12 is 9. So one bucket holds 9 litres.
Now we have 162 litres to store, at 9 litres to a bucket. What do we do?

ask.ifNot: We are asking how many times 9 litres fits into 162 litres. Counting how many times it fits is a division.

beats.say: 162 divided by 9 is 18.
So we need 18 buckets.
Check: 18 buckets with 9 litres in each. 18 times 9 is 162. And more water needed more buckets than 12, which makes sense.
So here is the plan. Find what one holds, then see how many of those you need.
72 men can do a piece of work in 40 hours. How many hours will 9 men take to do the same work?

board.text: 72 men do the work in 40 hours

beats.say: Think before any sum. With fewer men on the same job, will it take more time or less?

ask.ifNot: Picture it: fewer hands, the same job. Each man has more to do, so it takes longer. More time.

beats.say: So our answer must be bigger than 40. Keep that in your head. It will protect you from the trap in this question.
Find one first. One man alone would have to do the work of all 72 men, so he needs 72 times as long. 72 times 40 is 2880 hours.
Now 9 men share that work. What do we do with the 2880?

ask.ifNot: 9 men split the work between them, so each does a ninth of it. Sharing means dividing: 2880 divided by 9.

beats.say: 2880 divided by 9 is 320.
So 9 men take 320 hours.
Check with a shortcut. 72 men is 8 times as many as 9 men. So 9 men need 8 times as long, and 40 times 8 is 320.
The trap was to divide the 40 hours by 8 and get a smaller number. Fewer workers always means more time.
So when workers and time pull in opposite directions, multiply to find the time for one worker, then divide it among the workers you have.
A worker gets 504 rupees for 7 days of work. How many days must he work to get 792 rupees?
Notice what is asked: days, not rupees. And he earns the same amount every day.
What should we find first?

ask.ifNot: Find one first. Once we know the pay for 1 day, we can count how many days make 792 rupees.

beats.say: 504 rupees shared over 7 days. 504 divided by 7 is 72. So he earns 72 rupees a day.
Now, how many days at 72 rupees a day make 792 rupees?

ask.ifNot: We are asking how many times 72 rupees fits into 792 rupees. Counting how many times it fits is a division.

beats.say: 72 times 10 is 720, and one more 72 makes 792. So 792 divided by 72 is 11.
He must work 11 days.
Does it make sense? He wants more money than before, so he needs more days than 7. And 11 times 72 is 792. Yes.
Find the value of one, then use it. Here we divided twice: once to find one day's pay, and once to count the days.
A dozen pencils cost 18 rupees. How much would you pay for 18 pencils?
Look out: the number 18 appears twice here. One is rupees and the other is pencils. And first of all, how many pencils are in a dozen?

ask.ifNot: A dozen always means 12. So a dozen pencils is 12 pencils.

beats.say: So 12 pencils cost 18 rupees. Let's line it up in a table.
Find one first. One pencil costs 18 rupees shared among 12 pencils. 18 divided by 12 is 1.50, which is one and a half rupees.
Now we want 18 pencils. What do we do with the one and a half rupees?

ask.ifNot: 18 pencils, each costing one and a half rupees. 18 lots of the same amount means multiply.

beats.say: 18 times 1 is 18. 18 times a half is 9. Together that makes 27.
So 18 pencils cost 27 rupees.
Check another way. 18 pencils is a dozen plus half a dozen. A dozen costs 18 rupees, so half a dozen costs 9. And 18 plus 9 is 27.
When a question says dozen, turn it into 12 first. Then find one, and then find many.
Nine men complete a job in 32 days. How many days will 72 men take for the same job?

board.text: 9 men finish the work in 32 days

beats.say: Before any sum, think. With many more men on the job, will it take more days or fewer?

ask.ifNot: More hands make lighter work. With more men sharing the same job, it gets done sooner. Fewer days.

beats.say: So our answer must be smaller than 32. That one thought guards us against the trap in this question.
Find one first. If 9 men need 32 days, one man working alone would need 9 times as long. 9 times 32 is 288 days.
Now 72 men share that work. What do we do with the 288?

ask.ifNot: 72 men split the job between them, so it goes 72 times as fast. Sharing means dividing: 288 divided by 72.

beats.say: 288 divided by 72 is 4, because 72 times 4 is 288.
So 72 men finish the work in 4 days.
Check with a shortcut. 72 men is 8 times as many as 9 men. So they need only an eighth of the time, and 32 divided by 8 is 4.
When workers go up, days come down. Multiply to find the time for one worker, then divide it among all the workers.
After selling 15 dozen bananas, a man gains 45 rupees. How many dozen must he sell to gain 84 rupees?
Good news first. The question talks in dozens and asks for dozens. So we never need to count single bananas at all.
What should we find first?

ask.ifNot: Find one first. If we know the gain on 1 dozen, we can count how many dozens bring in 84 rupees.

beats.say: 45 rupees from 15 dozen. 45 divided by 15 is 3. So each dozen gains him 3 rupees.
He wants a gain of 84 rupees, at 3 rupees a dozen. What do we do?

ask.ifNot: Every dozen brings in 3 rupees. So we count how many times 3 goes into 84, and that is a division.

beats.say: 84 divided by 3 is 28.
He should sell 28 dozen bananas.
Check: 28 dozen at 3 rupees each. 28 times 3 is 84. And a bigger gain needed more dozens than 15, which makes sense.
So find the gain on one, then count how many ones you need. And only change the units when the question makes you.
Five people eat 1 kilogram of rice in a day. How much rice will 20 people eat in a week?

board.text: 5 people eat 1 kg of rice in a day
20 people in a week eat ? kg

beats.say: Two things change here: the number of people, and the number of days. We will handle one at a time. People first.
Look at the bars. How many groups of 5 people are there in 20 people?

spec.note: Each group of 5 eats 1 kg in a day

ask.ifNot: Count in fives until you reach 20, and you will have counted 4 times. So there are 4 groups of 5 people.

beats.say: 20 divided by 5 is 4. Each group of 5 eats 1 kilogram a day, so 4 groups eat 4 kilograms a day.
That was for one day. Now, how many days are there in a week?

ask.ifNot: A whole week runs from Monday round to Sunday. That is 7 days, not just the school days.

beats.say: 4 kilograms each day, for 7 days. 4 times 7 is 28.
So 20 people eat 28 kilograms of rice in a week.
Check it the other way round. One group of 5 eats 7 kilograms in a week. 4 such groups eat 7 times 4, which is 28.
When two things change, change one at a time. First the people, then the days.
A five litre can of liquid soap costs 370 rupees. What would a three litre can of the same soap cost?

board.text: A 5 litre can of soap costs ₹370

beats.say: Less soap, so it must cost less than 370 rupees. Keep that in mind as a safety check.
5 litres to 3 litres is an awkward jump. What do we find first?

ask.ifNot: Find one first. Once we know the cost of 1 litre, 3 litres is easy.

beats.say: 370 rupees shared over 5 litres. 370 divided by 5 is 74. So 1 litre costs 74 rupees.
And how do we get the cost of 3 litres?

ask.ifNot: 3 litres, at 74 rupees for each litre. 3 lots of 74 means multiply.

beats.say: 3 times 70 is 210, and 3 times 4 is 12. 210 plus 12 is 222.
So the three litre can costs 222 rupees.
Check. The other 2 litres would cost 2 times 74, which is 148. And 222 plus 148 is 370, the price of the full 5 litres.
The trap is to stop at 74, which is only 1 litre. Find one, then find many.
A machine makes 150 toys in one minute. How many toys does it make in 18 seconds?
Look at the units of time. One is in minutes, the other in seconds. What must we do before anything else?

ask.ifNot: We can't compare minutes with seconds. So first we write 1 minute as 60 seconds.

beats.say: 1 minute is 60 seconds. So the machine makes 150 toys in 60 seconds.
Find one first. In 1 second it makes 150 divided by 60. That is 2.5, two and a half toys each second.
And in 18 seconds?

ask.ifNot: Two and a half toys every second, for 18 seconds. That is 18 lots of 2.5, so we multiply.

beats.say: 18 times 2 is 36. 18 times a half is 9. 36 plus 9 is 45.
So the machine makes 45 toys in 18 seconds.
Check another way. 6 seconds is a tenth of a minute, so it gives a tenth of 150, which is 15 toys. 18 seconds is 3 lots of 6, and 3 times 15 is 45.
So make the units match, find one, then find many.
A man earned 120 rupees by selling 8 dozen mangoes. How much would he earn by selling 20 dozen?
More dozens sold, more rupees earned. So our answer must be bigger than 120.
8 dozen to 20 dozen is not a neat jump. What should we find first?

ask.ifNot: Find one first. From the earning on 1 dozen, we can reach 20 dozen, or any number of dozens.

beats.say: 120 rupees from 8 dozen. 120 divided by 8 is 15. He earns 15 rupees on each dozen.
And for 20 dozen?

ask.ifNot: 20 dozens, each earning 15 rupees. 20 lots of 15 means multiply.

beats.say: 2 times 15 is 30, so 20 times 15 is 300.
He would earn 300 rupees.
Check by a different path. 4 dozen is half of 8 dozen, so it earns half of 120, which is 60. 20 dozen is 5 lots of 4 dozen, and 5 times 60 is 300.
Find one, then find many. And notice we stayed in dozens the whole way, because the question did.
A man agrees to do a job in 30 days for 27,000 rupees. But he works for 18 days and then leaves. How much should he be paid?

board.text: He works only 18 days. Fair pay = ₹ ?

beats.say: What is fair? He should be paid for the days he worked, and not for the days he did not.
To pay him fairly, what should we find first?

ask.ifNot: The 27,000 rupees is for all 30 days. So first we find the pay for 1 day.

beats.say: 27,000 divided by 30 is 900, so one day of work earns 900 rupees. Careful: we divide by 30, the days the money was meant for, not by 18.
He worked 18 days. So what do we work out?

ask.ifNot: He earns 900 rupees for each day he worked, and he worked 18 days. So it is 18 times 900.

beats.say: 18 times 9 is 162, so 18 times 900 is 16,200.
A fair employer pays him 16,200 rupees.
Check. He missed 30 minus 18, that is 12 days, worth 12 times 900, which is 10,800 rupees. And 16,200 plus 10,800 is 27,000.
So for part of a job: find the pay for one day, then multiply by the days really worked.
A tailor has 37.5 metres of cloth. From every metre he makes 8 pieces. How many pieces can he make in all?

board.text: 37.5 m of cloth. 8 pieces from each metre.

beats.say: Picture one metre of cloth, cut into 8 pieces. Then another metre, and 8 more. So what do we do with 37.5 and 8?

spec.note: Every metre gives 8 pieces

ask.ifNot: Each metre gives 8 pieces, again and again for every metre. 8 pieces, 37.5 times over, means multiply.

beats.say: 37.5 is 37 whole metres and half a metre. Take the whole metres first. 37 times 8 is 296.
Now the half metre. Half of 8 pieces is 4 pieces.
296 plus 4 is 300. So he can make 300 pieces.
Now look at the choices: 320, 360, 400, or none of these. Our 300 is not there! What should we do?

choices: check our sum, then trust it
ask.ifNot: A careful answer does not change just because it is missing from the list. We check it, and if it holds, we trust it.

beats.say: So let's check. 300 pieces, at 8 from each metre: 300 divided by 8 is 37.5 metres. Exactly the cloth he has.
Our answer is 300 pieces. Since 300 is not on the list, we choose none of these.
Two things to keep. Multiply when every one gives the same number. And if your checked answer is not listed, none of these is a real answer.
One gross of notebooks is bought for 936 rupees. We need the cost of 48 notebooks.
There is a special word here: gross. How many is one gross?

ask.ifNot: A gross is a dozen dozens. That is 12 times 12, which is 144.

beats.say: A gross is a dozen dozens, and 12 times 12 is 144. So 144 notebooks cost 936 rupees.
Find one first. One notebook costs 936 divided by 144. Now, 144 times 6 is 864, and that leaves 72, which is exactly half of 144.
So 936 divided by 144 is 6 and a half. One notebook costs 6.50 rupees.
And how do we get the cost of 48 notebooks?

ask.ifNot: 48 notebooks, each costing 6.50 rupees. 48 lots of the same amount means multiply.

beats.say: 48 times 6 is 288. 48 times a half is 24. 288 plus 24 is 312.
So 48 notebooks cost 312 rupees.
Here is a lovely check. 48 is exactly one third of 144. So the cost should be one third of 936, and 936 divided by 3 is 312.
So unlock the special word first. Then find one, and then find many.
16 jugs can hold 1 decalitre of juice. How many jugs are needed to hold 15625 millilitres?
Two different units here, decalitres and millilitres. First, how much is 1 decalitre?

ask.ifNot: Deca means ten. So 1 decalitre is 10 litres.

beats.say: 1 decalitre is 10 litres, and each litre is 1000 millilitres. 10 times 1000 is 10,000 millilitres.
So 16 jugs hold 10,000 millilitres. Now both lines speak the same language.
Find one first. One jug holds 10,000 divided by 16, which is 625 millilitres.
Now, how many jugs of 625 millilitres do we need for 15625 millilitres?

ask.ifNot: We are counting how many times 625 fits into 15625. Counting how many times it fits is a division.

beats.say: 625 times 20 is 12500. 625 times 5 is 3125. Together they make 15625, so that is 20 and 5, 25 jugs.
We need 25 jugs.
Does it make sense? 15625 millilitres is more than 10,000, so we need more than 16 jugs. And 25 is more than 16.
So make the units match, find what one holds, then count how many you need.
12 men can complete a job in 54 days. How many men are needed to complete the same job in 24 days?

board.text: 12 men finish the work in 54 days

beats.say: We want the job done faster, in 24 days and not 54. Will we need more men, or fewer?

ask.ifNot: To finish sooner, we need more hands on the job. More men.

beats.say: So the answer must be bigger than 12. Now, how big is the whole job? Let's measure it in days of work for one man.
12 men, each working 54 days. 12 times 50 is 600, and 12 times 4 is 48. So 12 times 54 is 648 days of work.

board.text: Whole job = 648 days of work for 1 man

beats.say: These 648 days of work must fit into 24 days. How do we find the number of men?

ask.ifNot: Each man can give 24 days of work. So we count how many times 24 goes into 648, and that is a division.

beats.say: 24 times 25 is 600. That leaves 48, which is 24 times 2. And 25 and 2 make 27.
So 27 men are needed.
Check. Both teams must do the same amount of work. 12 times 54 is 648, and 27 times 24 is 648 too.
The trap is to think fewer days means fewer men. Less time always needs more workers. Find the whole job, then share it out.
A car travels 126 kilometres on 12 litres of petrol. How far will it go on 22 litres?
More petrol, so the car goes further. Our answer must be more than 126 kilometres.
What should we find first?

choices: how far it goes on 1 litre
ask.ifNot: Find one first. Once we know how far 1 litre takes the car, 22 litres is easy.

beats.say: 126 divided by 12. Now, 12 times 10 is 120, and the 6 left over is half of 12. So the car goes 10.5, ten and a half kilometres, on each litre.
And on 22 litres?

ask.ifNot: Every litre takes the car 10.5 kilometres, and there are 22 litres. 22 lots of 10.5 means multiply.

beats.say: 22 times 10 is 220. 22 times a half is 11. 220 plus 11 is 231.
The car will travel 231 kilometres.
Check another way. 22 litres is 12 litres and 10 more. The 12 litres give 126 kilometres, and 10 litres give 105. 126 plus 105 is 231.
Find how far one litre goes, then multiply by the litres you have. Find one, then find many.
Three dozen mangoes cost 1800 rupees. How much would 26 mangoes cost?
Careful with the units: the price is for dozens, but we are asked about single mangoes. A dozen is 12. So how many mangoes are in three dozen?

ask.ifNot: Three dozen means 3 lots of 12. And 3 times 12 is 36.

beats.say: 3 times 12 is 36. So 36 mangoes cost 1800 rupees.
Find one first. One mango costs 1800 divided by 36. Now, 36 times 5 is 180, so 36 times 50 is 1800. One mango costs 50 rupees.
And 26 mangoes?

ask.ifNot: 26 mangoes, at 50 rupees each. 26 lots of 50 means multiply.

beats.say: 26 times 5 is 130, so 26 times 50 is 1300.
So 26 mangoes cost 1300 rupees.
Check. 26 is 10 fewer than 36. Those 10 mangoes would cost 10 times 50, which is 500 rupees. And 1800 minus 500 is 1300.
The trap is to stop at the price of a dozen. Go all the way down to one mango, then build back up.
One gross of cricket balls costs 32,400 rupees. What will 85 cricket balls cost?
The word to unlock is gross. A dozen is 12, and a gross is a dozen dozens: 12 times 12, which is 144.
So 144 balls cost 32,400 rupees, and we want 85 balls. What do we find first?

ask.ifNot: 85 is not a neat number of dozens. So we go all the way down to 1 ball, and build up from there.

beats.say: One ball costs 32,400 divided by 144, which is 225 rupees. We can be sure by multiplying back: 144 times 225 is 32,400.
And how do we get the cost of 85 balls?

ask.ifNot: 85 balls, at 225 rupees each. 85 lots of 225 means multiply.

beats.say: Split the 85 into 80 and 5. 80 times 225 is 18,000. And 5 times 225 is 1125.
So 85 cricket balls cost 19,125 rupees.
Does it look right? 85 balls is a bit more than half a gross. And 19,125 rupees is a bit more than half of 32,400. Good.
So unlock the special word, find the cost of one, then find the cost of many.
15 men can do a job in 28 days. If it must be done in 20 days, how many more men are needed?

board.text: 15 men do the work in 28 days
To finish in 20 days: how many MORE men?

beats.say: Read the last words slowly: how many more men. Not how many men in all. Let's underline that, so we don't forget.
First, how big is the whole job? 15 men, each working 28 days. How do we count the days of work?

ask.ifNot: Each of the 15 men puts in 28 days. So the whole job is 15 lots of 28 days of work.

beats.say: 10 times 28 is 280, and 5 times 28 is 140. Together, 420. The whole job is 420 days of work for one man.
Now those 420 days of work must fit into 20 days. 420 divided by 20 is 21. So 21 men are needed.
Is 21 our answer?

ask.ifNot: The question asks how many more men. 15 are already there, so we want only the extra ones: 21 minus 15.

beats.say: 21 minus 15 is 6.
So 6 more men are needed.
Check. 21 men for 20 days is 420 days of work, the same as 15 men for 28 days. The job matches.
Two things to keep. Fewer days needs more men. And answer the question that was asked: here, the extra men, not the total.
